description: A dwarf evergreen shrub 10-30 cm tall that forms dense mats of upright stems crowded with short, needle-like, dark green leaves, topped in midsummer by clusters of rose-purple, saucer-shaped flowers. It grows in the alpine and subalpine high country, about 2400-3600 m, on rocky slopes, lake shores, meadow edges and in the shelter of boulders and krummholz where snow lies late.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen under the snow, which it needs for protection from the winter wind.
season_notes.spring: Still under snow until June or July; the mats emerge dark green and flattened.
season_notes.summer: Rose-purple flowers crowd the stem tips, July-August, worked by bumblebees.
season_notes.fall: Small dry capsules split; the mats bronze slightly in the first frosts.

notes: Called purple mountain heath by Calscape and Brewer's mountain heather by others; 'red mountain heather' is the common Sierra guidebook name. The gooseberry template is only a stand-in for a low, many-stemmed woody shrub; the card makes it a much lower, denser, evergreen mat of tiny linear leaves (6-12 mm) and turns the template's berries off. 'lanceolate' at 1 cm is the nearest leaf shape; the true look is a bottle-brush of needle-like leaves on each stem, which needs a needle card the broadleaf path does not use. It grows in snow-protected spots and wet ground: the species mix should favour lake shores, boulder lees and late-snow hollows. No wildlife forage use was read; it is little eaten. The Jepson eFlora page could not be read (it asked for a human check); elevations are the drafter's knowledge.
